label: prf:s5-equivariant-torus-knots
title: Proof of s5 equivariant torus knots
html:
An equivariant embedding requires \mathbb{Z}_s \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Aut}(\Sigma) = S_5. The cyclic symmetry of the knot must match a symmetry of the ambient surface. An injection \mathbb{Z}_s \hookrightarrow S_5 exists if and only if S_5 contains an element of order s. The orders of elements in S_5 are the least common multiples of the parts of integer partitions of 5.

See Table.

The realised orders in S_5 are \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}. The condition \gcd(2, s) = 1 forces odd s \geq 3. This restricts the possible orders to \{3, 5\}. \square

The monodromy test. An element of order 2s with s odd and s \geq 3 must have order 6, 10 or 30 among the divisors of 60. An element whose order is divisible by 5 is a 5-cycle, of order exactly 5, so orders 10 and 30 do not occur. Order 6 is realised by a transposition times a disjoint 3-cycle. Hence the monodromy test holds only for s = 3. \square

Corollary. Among torus knots T_{2, s} with s \geq 3, exactly two admit cyclic-symmetry-preserving embeddings into \Sigma_4 (Bring's surface): T_{2, 3} and T_{2, 5}. Any other torus knot of this family either breaks the symmetry in the embedding or fails to embed topologically (Seifert genus > 4, or s \geq 11).

Comparison with genus-based embedding. Pure topological (Seifert-genus) embedding into \Sigma_4 admits four knots: T_{2, 3}, T_{2, 5}, T_{2, 7}, and T_{2, 9}. The stronger equivariant criterion retains only T_{2, 3} and T_{2, 5}. The knots T_{2, 7} and T_{2, 9} are topologically admissible but symmetry-broken.
